glossary.meaning: A bishop, for us, is not an officer of some wider institution, dropped into a posting. He is given a people. He preaches to them and baptizes them, and when they fail it is not a problem he manages but a wound he carries. The charge runs both ways: he answers for his flock, and his flock can stand in front of his seat and refuse to leave until he hears them.

The lapsed are our own people who complied with the order to sacrifice during the persecution -- some by sacrificing, some only by paying for a certificate that said they had. They are not strangers and not enemies. They sat where we sit, and now they are asking to come back.
Discipline is the road; reconciliation is the arrival. What matters is that it is a road at all. There is an order to it, the order takes time, and everyone can see it.
For us, a confessor is one who was interrogated for the Name, did not deny it, and lived. In Cyprian's time, that standing could rival a bishop's own authority.
For us, communion is a formal standing within the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of it for thinking differently.

A certificate is a letter from a confessor, given to a lapsed person. It asks for peace, or says peace is granted. Cyprian wanted each one to name the person. Some named one person and then let in his own people too, without naming them.

pull_quotes.text: I grieve, brothers, I grieve with you. My own integrity and my personal soundness do not lure me into soothing my griefs. That is because it is the shepherd who is wounded most deeply when his flock is wounded. I hold each one of you close to my heart, and I share the heavy burden of sorrow and mourning. I wail with those who wail, I weep with those who weep...

None of us sets himself up as a bishop over other bishops, and none of us uses a tyrant's terror to force a colleague into obedience. Every bishop has his own right to judge, in keeping with the freedom and power allowed to him. He can no more be judged by another bishop than he himself can judge another. Instead, let us all wait for the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the only one who has the power both to place us in the government of His Church and to judge how we conduct ourselves there.

The visible form of a branch can exist even when it is separated from the vine. But the unseen life of the root can only be had in the vine. So the bodily sacraments can give “the form of godliness.” Even those who are separated from the unity of Christ’s Body carry and celebrate them. But the unseen, spiritual power of godliness cannot be in them at all. In the same way, feeling does not stay with a person's limb when it is cut off from the body.

You share communion with the members of the Apostles. You share communion with the shrines of the holy martyrs, who are spread over the whole world. And you belong to my care, so that I may give a good account of you. You know what my whole account is. “Lord, You know that I have spoken. You know that I have not kept silent. You know in what spirit I have spoken. You know that I have wept before You when I spoke and was not heard.”

cite.text: In our earliest years, those who had confessed Christ and suffered for it made a claim of their own. Their suffering, they held, gave them standing to ask peace for some who had failed the test they passed. We took that claim in earnest. Their suffering was real, and so was what it carried. And it still had to be answered by something steadier than one man's word, however real his suffering had been: a name set down, then examined before the whole congregation and with its judgment. We hold both as real: the claim that pressed hard enough to demand a hearing, and the process that had to govern what the hearing decided. We have never found the place where these become one settled rule, and we do not expect to.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: When someone wronged the community, how was it handled — and could they come back?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: They could come back, and the way back was walked where everyone could see it. Their name was set down first. Cyprian wrote to the confessors, those who had suffered for the faith. He warned that a certificate taking in some man together with his own people let too many in at once. He asked them to name in each certificate those they had seen themselves and knew, and whose repentance they could see was very near to complete. Then came the waiting, and it was not a formality. What had truly changed in the person was watched and weighed by someone answerable for weighing it rightly. It was not granted the moment anyone felt moved to grant it, and it was not handed out on request. At the end, it was not settled between two people in private. The same congregation that watched the failure received the person back, together, in the open.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: That sounds like you're making them prove themselves before you'll trust they've changed. Isn't real forgiveness supposed to be unconditional?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We asked ourselves that, and we never found the single answer that settles it without losing something true on one side. During the persecution a confessor among us, Celerinus, wrote to another confessor, Lucian, who was in prison. He told Lucian he was in the midst of great trouble. His own sister had sacrificed. He grieved for her as for a death, a death of the spirit. He asked Lucian to grieve with him, and to help her and two other women, Numeria and Candida. He made the case for them: they had repented, and there were works to point to. Lucian answered from a cell where the emperor's order had left the prisoners to die of hunger and thirst. He granted the peace they asked for, on one condition. Each case had to be set before the bishop, and the sin openly confessed. The confessors held that their suffering gave them standing to ask for peace. Lucian's own letter still sent every case to the bishop. Whether Celerinus's sister walked the whole road home, our record does not say.

cite.text: We can argue that a colleague's ruling was wrong, at length, and still keep him at our table. One of our bishops said so when he opened the council that would settle the hardest question in the room. No bishop, he said, sets himself up as a bishop of bishops. None forces a colleague to obey. Every bishop has his own proper right of judgment. At that same council, he said we judge no one, and reject no one from communion, for thinking differently from us. A century and a half later, another of our bishops argued at book length that the ruling made that day was wrong. He never once put the man who made it outside our communion. In our own first years, we had seen separation from the inside. A deacon's faction gathered apart while our bishop was away in hiding. In those same years, a rival bishop was set up at Rome over a disputed election. We do not pretend those separations never happened. We hold our rule against separation knowing, from our own record, what it costs when it breaks.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did your people never settle?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: What a font gives, when the hand that fills it comes from outside the one church. We answered it twice, by two of our own bishops, a century and a half apart, and the two answers are opposites. Cyprian held that nothing valid is given outside at all. So the person comes to the water in the church and is baptized for the first time. Augustine held that something real is given even there, though it does the person no good until they come inside. So we bring them in, and let what they already carry begin to work. We do not resolve which of them was right. Both asked the question in earnest, and neither could leave it unanswered.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: So which one do you actually believe?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We keep both answers. Augustine argued at book length that Cyprian's ruling was wrong. He never once said that Cyprian stood outside our communion. He reached for a branch to say what he meant. Cut from the vine, a branch keeps its shape. It does not keep its life. That, he held, is what a baptism given outside is: the true form, carried by people cut off from the one body it lives in. He said the washing is not repeated for them, since the form was not missing even while they were outside. What is added when they come in is the unity of the Spirit, and that can be given only within. Cyprian's answer stands as it was: nothing valid is given outside. Nearly a century and a half lay between the two answers.

cite.text:
Between the two phases, the bishop's office changed its legal position. At first it had no legal standing at all. Later it could ask the state to act against a rival communion.

The outside change itself is documented. One element is contested: not whether the shift happened, but whether its consequence belongs among the world's inner forces or its outside pressures. Placing it as an inner force follows a judgement we made earlier, not a settled finding.

The shift is the old condition of illegality turned upside down, the same fact appearing at both ends of the story with the opposite sign. What a bishop could do had changed, though what a bishop was had not -- Cyprian never asked the magistrate for anything, and a century and a third later, the emperors could be asked, and eventually were.

We considered whether the shift itself was one of this world's own central concerns. It is not, because nothing in this world actually organizes itself around the shift. It changes the tools a bishop has, not what a bishop is. A separate look from the ethical and legal side reached the same conclusion. So it is kept as a real force, with an impact deliberately limited in proportion to its weight. A rival communion, the Donatist church, is what made the new state power worth using.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Your church used power against Christians who disagreed. Defend that.

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We will not defend it as plainly right, and we will not disown it. In our later years the Donatists, a rival church, stood in our own towns and claimed to be the only true one. Augustine moved across a hard question in three stages. By his own later account, he first held that no one should be forced into the church. Words only, argument only, never compulsion. Later, he and his colleagues in council asked the emperors for a narrow measure. It would reach the Donatist clergy only in places where our own people had already suffered violence over the dispute. It was not even granted. A broader law reached the same end first. Later still, he defended a fuller compulsion at length, when it was already in force. Looking back, he tells it as a change of mind. Whether it was a true change of heart, or the way he chose to tell his own story afterward, we cannot say from inside him.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: So does that mean you think using force against them was right?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We do not call it plainly right, and we do not hide it either. What moved him, he says, was not the arguments of the men who disagreed with him. It was the cases his colleagues set in front of him. The first was his own town. It had once stood wholly with the other side. Fear of the emperors' edicts brought it back to the one communion, and it stayed. Then many other towns were named to him. That is what persuaded him, by his own account. We hold it as his, argued at real length, and we hold it beside his first view, that no one should be forced. Which of his three stages did you have in mind when you asked us to defend it?

quiet.statement: The lapsed are the one group our whole first crisis was actually about, and they are the one group who left us nothing in their own words. We can tell you what was decided about a person who yielded under persecution, and how fiercely, and by whom. We cannot tell you why a person gave way, what they told themselves while they did it, or whether they judged the terms of their own return just. Every account we have of the lapsed is a bishop's account of them, written to decide what should be done, never their own.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

dates.display: Cyprian's own deacon, present with him at his banishment to Curubis; wrote The Life and Passion of Cyprian after his bishop's execution in 258, the first Christian biography

a confessor -- imprisoned under persecution and did not deny Christ; wrote to Lucian, a fellow confessor in prison, asking that his own sister and two other women be received back to communion (Ep. XX)

converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

dates.display: Augustine's own friend for nearly forty years; bishop of Calama in his own right; physically present at Augustine's deathbed in 430, one of those Augustine 'asked of us who were present'; wrote the Vita Augustini, the source for the psalms on the wall and for the account of the people seizing Augustine at Hippo

who_speaks.text: Five figures carry this world's voice. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, speaks in his own letters and books, as a shepherd wounded in his flock's wound. Pontius, his deacon, went with him into exile and wrote of his life and death. Celerinus, a confessor, wrote in the persecution, grieving for a sister who had sacrificed. Augustine, bishop of Hippo, preached to one congregation for decades. He argued with Cyprian across a century and a half. Possidius, his friend, stood by as he died.

documented_stories.teaser: Carthage makes a man its bishop while he is still new to the faith. Five of the clergy object. His deacon calls it God's judgment, shown in the people's favour.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How we came to treat a recent convert's own election, over his reluctance, as God's own judgment made visible
documented_stories.telling:
Our deacon Pontius wrote the life of Cyprian after his bishop had been put to death. He said it would take too long to tell all that Cyprian did, and that one fact was proof enough of his good works.

"By the judgment of God and the favour of the people, he was chosen for the sacred office and the rank of bishop. He was still newly baptized and, as people thought, a beginner." Pontius did not soften this. He pressed it, describing Cyprian as still in the untaught season of his spiritual life.

Cyprian did not reach for the office. When the whole people leapt forward in love for him, Pontius says, he humbly stepped back. He gave way to older men and thought himself unworthy. A crowd of the brothers besieged the doors of his house.

For Pontius, God's judgment and the people's favour were not two claims pulling against each other. The people's favour was how God's judgment became visible to us. Pontius does not say how the people made their favour known.

Years later, rivals who had never accepted him renewed their attack. Cyprian answered them in a letter to us. They still carried, he wrote, "that old venom against my office as bishop, which means against your suffrage and against God's judgment."

Only Pontius says that Cyprian was newly baptized when he was chosen, and no other witness of ours confirms or corrects it. Pontius was also writing in praise of his own bishop.
documented_stories.title: Chosen While Still New to the Faith

documented_stories.teaser: Celerinus grieves that his sister has sacrificed. He asks Lucian, a confessor held in prison, to grant peace to her and to two other women. Lucian grants it to the two women by name, on condition that each case goes before the bishop.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How one confessor asked another, not a bishop, to seek peace for his sister and two other women
documented_stories.telling:
Celerinus was one of our confessors, a man who had been imprisoned and had not denied Christ. He wrote to Lucian, another confessor, who was still in prison.

"Grieve with me over my sister's death, a death of the spirit," he wrote. "In this time of ruin she has fallen away from Christ. For she has sacrificed and angered our Lord, as seems clear to us." She was still alive in body. He would weep, he said, until help came through Lucian or through the martyrs Lucian would ask. Her own brother does not give her name, and no word of hers survives.

He also asked the martyrs' pardon for two women Lucian knew, Numeria and Candida. He pointed to their repentance and to the good works they had done for our banished colleagues.

Of Candida he said more. She had given gifts so that she would not have to sacrifice. She seems only to have gone up as far as the Tria Fata, and then come back down. "So I know she has not sacrificed." Still, both letters call what the women did a great sin.

Lucian's answer came back from the prison, where the emperor had ordered the confessors put to death by hunger and thirst. "But now we have reached the brightness itself," he wrote.

He granted the request in the name of the martyr Paulus and the other martyrs, with one condition. Each case was to be set before the bishop and the sin openly confessed. Then, he asked, "let not only these women have peace, but also those whom you know to be dear to our heart."

He greeted friends by name and left the rest out, "because I am already tired. So they must forgive me."
documented_stories.title: A Confessor Writes to a Confessor in Prison

documented_stories.teaser: Numidicus urges others to die for the faith and sees his wife burn with them. His daughter finds him alive under the stones. Cyprian adds him to the clergy of Carthage.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How our bishop added to our presbyters a confessor who had not wanted to survive
documented_stories.telling:
Cyprian wrote to us with news that he said belonged to the joy of us all. He was adding Numidicus to the presbyters of Carthage, and he wanted us to know who the man was.

"By his urging he sent a great number of martyrs ahead of himself, killed by stones and by fire." His own wife died with them. "With joy he watched his wife, who stayed at his side, burned with the others," Cyprian wrote, and then corrected himself. "I should rather say she was preserved."

That correction is not a slip, for we did not count a martyr's death as a loss to be consoled. We named it as a completion, even at the cost of sounding cold.

"He himself was half burned, buried under stones and left for dead." His daughter came looking for her father's body "with the anxious care of love." He was found half dead, pulled out and revived. The letter does not say where she searched.

Cyprian adds one more clause. "Against his will, he stayed behind the companions he himself had sent ahead." One manuscript and the older printed editions read "unconquered" here instead of "against his will."

Cyprian gave the reason he saw for it. The Lord meant to add Numidicus to our clergy, and to fill the ranks of our presbyters, left thin by the fall of some.

None of the three left a word of their own. We do not know what the wife thought, what the daughter found, or what Numidicus said when they revived him.
documented_stories.title: The Presbyter Who Had Not Wanted to Survive
documented_stories.when: Cyprian's years as bishop (the letter gives no year)

documented_stories.teaser: Christians are carried off as captives. The clergy and people of Carthage collect a hundred thousand sesterces to ransom them. No one knows whether the ransom worked.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How we sent a hundred thousand sesterces to ransom our captive brethren
documented_stories.telling:
Word came that our brothers and sisters had been carried off and were held captive among barbarians. Eight bishops in Numidia wrote to Cyprian about it. He names them one by one: Januarius, Maximus, Proculus, Victor, Modianus, Nemesianus, Nampulus and Honoratus.

His reply opens without composure. "With great grief of mind, and not without tears, dearest brothers, I have read your letter."

His argument was not about charity but about who the captives were. He quoted Paul: "As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Then he drew the conclusion. "So Christ is to be seen in our captive brothers. He who redeemed us from the danger of death is to be redeemed from the danger of captivity."

He named the test this set for us. "Will each of us do for another what he would want done for himself, if he were held captive among barbarians?"

Then he said what we were sending. "So we have sent you a sum of one hundred thousand sesterces." It came from the gifts of our clergy and people. The bishops were to hand it out there as carefully as they could.

He thanked them for asking us, since they had offered us "fruitful fields in which to sow the seeds of our hope."

We do not know whether the ransom worked. Cyprian never wrote of the outcome, and no reply from the eight bishops survives. The story ends with the money leaving Carthage.
documented_stories.title: A Hundred Thousand Sesterces for the Captives
documented_stories.when: Cyprian's years as bishop, 248/249 to 258 (the letter gives no year)

documented_stories.teaser: While the city flees its sick, Cyprian tells his people to help everyone, not only their own. Only his deacon's account keeps the sermon.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How our bishop met a plague by teaching us to love even our enemies, and to help everyone, not only our own
documented_stories.telling:
Our deacon Pontius was there. Only his life of our bishop tells of the sermon and the help that followed. He wrote it in praise of the man who preached.

"Afterwards a dreadful plague broke out," he wrote. It went through the houses of the trembling city one after another, carrying off countless people every day.

"Everyone shuddered and fled, and shunned the contagion. They wickedly put out their own people." All over the city, Pontius says, there lay "no longer bodies but the corpses of many."

Our bishop gathered us in one place and preached. He began with the good that mercy does, and then went further. There was nothing remarkable, he said, in caring only for our own.

To be perfect, we must do more than the tax collector or the pagan. We must love even our enemies, and pray for those who persecute us. God makes His sun rise and sends rain to feed the seed. He shows these kindnesses not only to His own people. "It is right for us," Cyprian said, "to live up to our birth."

Then, Pontius says, good was done to all people, not only to those of the household of faith. Many who were too poor to give money gave their own labour instead.

Tobias, Pontius says, gathered the bodies of those the king had killed, but only those of his own race. More was done here.

Pontius does not say whether those who persecuted us were among the people helped. No one outside his account describes the relief, and no pagan of Carthage left a word about it.
documented_stories.title: Love for Enemies in a Time of Plague

documented_stories.teaser: Two early texts tell how Cyprian was put to death, with his people watching. They agree on most of it, and differ on who tied the cloth over his eyes.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How two early texts tell the death of our great bishop Cyprian, and where they differ
documented_stories.telling:
Our great bishop Cyprian was executed on 14 September 258. Two early texts tell his death. One is a saint's life by his deacon Pontius. The other is the Acta, an early Christian compilation built around the records of his hearings, whose compiler is unnamed.

On his last night Cyprian was held in an officer's house, with Pontius and his friends beside him. "Meanwhile the whole people kept watch before the officer's door," Pontius writes.

Pontius says the sentence called Cyprian a standard-bearer of the sect and an enemy of the gods. With his blood, it said, discipline would begin to be made firm. The Acta gives the sentence in nearly the same words. On the sentence, the two texts are not independent witnesses. Only the Acta gives his answer: "Thanks be to God."

Then, the Acta says, the brothers kept crying, "Let us be beheaded with him too." Pontius does not quote the cry, but he calls the people blessed for suffering with their bishop in words spoken aloud.

In the field of Sextus, the Acta says, Cyprian took off his cloak and knelt in prayer. He told his people to give the executioner twenty-five gold pieces.

The two texts differ on the cloth over his eyes. Pontius says Cyprian bound his eyes with his own hands. The Acta says he covered them with his hand but could not tie the strips himself. So the presbyter Julianus and the subdeacon Julianus tied them. We do not choose between the two.

Some things only Pontius tells. People had climbed into the trees to see, so that, as with Zacchaeus, he was gazed at from the branches. The executioner could hardly grip the blade with trembling fingers until, Pontius says, the hour of glory strengthened his hand from above. That is Pontius's telling, and the Acta says nothing of it.
documented_stories.title: Two Accounts of a Bishop's Death

documented_stories.teaser: The bishop who taught that even good Christians must repent before death has the psalms of penitence hung by his bed. He reads them and weeps.
documented_stories.tellable_as: How the man who taught that even good Christians must repent before death did it himself
documented_stories.telling:
Possidius was Augustine's friend for nearly forty years, and he was in the house at the end. The Vandals were besieging Hippo, and in the third month of the siege Augustine fell ill with a fever.

In private talk, Possidius says, Augustine often taught one thing. Even after baptism, good Christians and priests ought not leave this life without fitting repentance.

"And he did this himself in the last illness of which he died. He ordered the very few penitential Psalms of David to be copied for him. As he lay in bed during his sickness, he would look at these sheets hanging on the wall and read them. And he wept freely and constantly."

About ten days before the end, he asked those who were there to let no one in. The only exceptions were the doctors and those who brought his food. The request was kept, and he had all that time free for prayer.

Up to that last illness he had preached in the church without ceasing. At the end his sight and hearing were unimpaired. While Possidius and the others stood by, watching and praying, "he slept with his fathers," in the words of Scripture.

He made no will, because as a poor man of God he had nothing to make one from. He had ordered that the church's library and all its books be carefully kept for those who came after.

Possidius is the only witness to these last weeks. The death and the siege are known from outside Hippo, but no second source shows us the sickroom.
documented_stories.title: Psalms of Penitence on the Wall
documented_stories.when: August 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

floor_note.text: This church confessed Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, our Lord. It went on to confess the Holy Spirit, completing the Trinity of the one Godhead. That faith did meet real opponents. Late in Augustine's years, an Arian bishop named Maximinus debated him at Hippo over the Trinity. But this church's sharpest arguments were rarely about the creed. They were about rites: who may baptize, whose baptism counts, and how someone who failed comes back to the table.

highlights.note: Christians who gave in to the order to sacrifice in 250. Some sacrificed, and some bought a paper saying they had.
Christians who were questioned, did not deny Christ, and lived. In Cyprian's time their standing could rival a bishop's.
Letters a confessor gave a lapsed person. They asked for peace, or said it was granted. The quarrel was over who decides.
Cyprian's phrase for what no bishop may be. Each bishop judges for himself and answers to Christ.
A real standing inside the one body. It can be lost and given back. Cyprian held it should survive sharp disagreement.
A rival church in the same North African towns, with its own bishops. It baptized again those who joined it.
The view Augustine fought, that a person's own effort is enough without grace. Whether Pelagius held it so is disputed.
The bishops met at Carthage under Cyprian in 256. They ruled that those baptized outside the church be baptized in it.
The Roman emperor who began a new attack on Christians in 257. Under his rule Cyprian was sent away, then put to death.
Cyprian's deacon. He went with him into exile and later wrote the story of his life and death.
Bishop of Calama and Augustine's friend for nearly forty years. He wrote the Life of Augustine.
A people who crossed from Spain into Africa in the late 420s. In 430 their army besieged Hippo.
The chief city of its province and Cyprian's see. Its ruins lie in today's Tunis, in Tunisia.
A port in North Africa, where Augustine was bishop. It is now the city of Annaba, in Algeria.
The town where Cyprian was held in exile under Valerian. Its site lies in today's Tunisia.

legacy.text: Augustine's books outlived this world. Inside his own church, nothing else depended on how the argument over grace came out. Later it became a foundation of Western Christian thought. Catholic and Protestant readers still draw on it, and they still disagree about what it means.

The church that kept both bishops' books kept Cyprian even where it judged him wrong, on baptism. This world has no single living heir. Its ordinary work, a pastor answerable for one local flock, makes it an ancestor of the Western church as it was before that church divided.

read_first.note: Cyprian's book on those who gave way in the persecution of 250. It sets out the road back, and why the bishop holds it.

source.citation: Cyprian of Carthage, On the Lapsed (De Lapsis), Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. V

read_first.note: Cyprian's letters, with some written to him. They include two confessors' own letters and his account of his election.

source.citation: Cyprian of Carthage, The Epistles, including letters to Cyprian from Rome, Cornelius, the confessors and Firmilian of Caesarea, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. V

read_first.note: The Life of Augustine, written by his friend Possidius, who was with him when he died.

source.citation: Possidius of Calama, Sancti Augustini Vita Scripta a Possidio Episcopo (Life of Augustine), ed. and trans. Herbert T. Weiskotten (Princeton: Princeton University Press; London: Humphrey Milford, Oxford University Press, 1919)

relations_summary.text: The rival Donatist church shared this world's provinces and its century, and it appealed to Cyprian himself. The two answered one question in opposite ways. When bishops cannot settle a disagreement, do they keep communion or build a rival church? The Donatists built their own. This church kept its bond, even with the bishop it judged wrong. Its law looks different from an imperial church's, too. There, church law orders the relations of sees and the state. Here, it exists to bring a failed member home.

sourcing.text: This world keeps more of its own words than most. Cyprian and Augustine both speak at length, as bishops of this church, not as quotations in an opponent's book. The problem is who else speaks. Almost no one outside the clergy left an account. No ordinary believer wrote about an ordinary Sunday. No woman's own writing survives, and none of the lapsed explained themselves. The church buildings are known mostly from one letter, not from excavation. Most of the reading here is done in English translations from the 19th century.

story.text: This is the ordinary church of Latin-speaking Roman North Africa, from about 246 to 430, and it lived in two cities. Carthage was the chief see of its province and the largest Latin Christian city outside Rome. Hippo Regius was a port further along the coast, in the church province of Numidia. The name used here is a modern label, because this church had no special name for itself. It saw itself simply as the church, doing the ordinary work of caring for the people in front of it.

At its center stood one plain fact: a bishop was given a particular people, in one place, and he answered for them. He preached to them week after week, taught those preparing for baptism, washed them at the font and fed them at the table. When they failed, it was his own wound before it was a case to judge. Cyprian put it in one image: the shepherd is wounded most deeply when his flock is wounded. The tie ran both ways. The people could call a man to the office against his will, and they could crowd before his seat and refuse to go home.

Cyprian was a trained public speaker who turned to the church in about 246. Within two or three years the people of Carthage made him their bishop by acclaim. He was still newly baptized, and five presbyters, the clergy just below a bishop, opposed him. He later named what had put him there: the people's voice, joined to God's judgment. A century and a half later, Augustine's path ran the same way. In 391 the congregation at Hippo seized him and had him made a presbyter while he wept.

In 250 came the first persecution enforced across the whole empire by plan. It did not mainly demand that Christians give up their faith, but a recorded act of sacrifice to the gods, proved by a certificate. Some Christians sacrificed, and others paid to have the sacrifice recorded without making it. Both groups were called the lapsed. They were the church's own people, and now they asked to come back. To shut them out for good would say that one hour under pressure decides a life. To let them straight back would say the hour meant nothing.

So the church kept a road back. A failed member's name was set down, and what had truly changed in the person was watched and weighed. At the end, the same people who saw the fall received the person home, in the open. A rival claim pressed against this road. Confessors were Christians who had been questioned, had not denied Christ, and had lived. Some of them wrote certificates of peace for the lapsed, and Cyprian complained that thousands went out every day. He held that the church's peace was not any one sufferer's to give, and that tension was never fully settled.

Plague came too, from about 249 to 262. Cyprian's deacon Pontius describes a city where people fled the sick and left bodies where they fell. Cyprian called his congregation together and told them that caring for their own was nothing remarkable. They should help everyone, their enemies included. The plague produced no new rule and no new structure, only a sermon and a short book on dying called On Mortality.

In 256 Cyprian opened a council of African bishops on a hard question. If someone was baptized outside the church, was that baptism real? The council held that nothing valid is given outside, so such a person must be baptized in the church for the first time. Opening the council, Cyprian said that no bishop sets himself up as a bishop of bishops. Each has his own right to judge, and no one is put out of communion for thinking differently.

Persecution returned under the emperor Valerian. Cyprian was sent into exile at Curubis, and then brought back to trial. On 14 September 258 he was put to death by the sword. He had spent years deciding what to do with those who failed the first test. The second test took him, and he did not fail it.

Then this church's own voice goes quiet for about 133 years, from 258 to 391. Much happened in those years, but what survives of them comes mostly from the rival Donatist church and its opponents, not from this church's pastors. Nine old sermons, printed in a scholarly edition in 1917, may date from those years. They have not yet been assessed in building this world, so the silence is held as an open question, not a settled fact.

The second voice is Augustine. He came to the faith in 386 and was baptized at Milan in 387. At Hippo he was made a presbyter in 391 and bishop in 395 or 396. He preached to the same congregation for decades, and many of his sermons survive. By then a rival church stood in the same towns, the Donatists, with their own bishops in the same sees. They baptized again those who came over to them, and they named Cyprian's ruling as their warrant.

Augustine answered the font question the other way. Something real is given even outside the church, he argued, though it does the person no good until they come inside. So such people were received, not baptized again. In his book On Baptism he argued at length that Cyprian's ruling was wrong. Yet he never placed Cyprian outside the church. Disagreeing with a colleague, even a revered one, was not a reason to separate. The font was answered twice, and both answers stayed inside one communion.

On using force against the rival church, Augustine's mind moved in three stages. By his own later account, he first held that no one should be forced into the church. Then he and his fellow bishops asked the emperors for a narrow measure, and it was not granted. Later still, he defended a fuller use of force that was already in place. He told it as a change of mind. Scholars still dispute whether it was one, or a later way of telling the story. Cyprian never asked the state for anything.

In the 410s and 420s a second fight took hold, over grace. Augustine argued that no one's own will, left to itself, is enough to stand right before God. Whatever good a person does was given to them first. He wrote thirteen works against what he called the Pelagian view. Whether Pelagius himself held that view in that form is disputed. This argument belongs only to Augustine's years, and Cyprian never argued it in those terms.

In 430 a Vandal army besieged Hippo, and Augustine fell ill in the third month of the siege. His friend Possidius, bishop of Calama, was in the house. He tells how Augustine had the shortest psalms of penitence copied out and hung on the wall, and read them from his bed, weeping. He died on 28 August 430. The siege of Hippo closes this world's years.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

voices.hedge: His own letters let us hear him directly, and at length. But the story of his rise and his death comes mostly from his deacon, who wrote in praise. That he was newly baptized when chosen rests on that one witness alone.
voices.text: Cyprian was a trained public speaker who turned to the church around 246. Carthage made him its bishop within a few years, while he was still newly baptized. He led his people through persecution, plague and schism. A large collection of his letters survives, with some written to him, along with treatises such as On the Lapsed. He spoke of a shepherd wounded in his own flock's wound. He was put to death under Valerian in 258.

dates.display: Cyprian's own deacon, present with him at his banishment to Curubis; wrote The Life and Passion of Cyprian after his bishop's execution in 258, the first Christian biography

voices.hedge: Pontius wrote to praise his bishop, and he shaped the death on patterns from Scripture. Some of his details have no second witness. Scholars dispute how far his account can be read as plain testimony.
voices.text: Pontius was Cyprian's deacon. He went with his bishop into exile at Curubis and was with him on his last night. After the execution in 258 he wrote The Life and Passion of Cyprian, counted the first Christian biography. It holds the election, the plague sermon and the death.

dates.display: a confessor -- imprisoned under persecution and did not deny Christ; wrote to Lucian, a fellow confessor in prison, asking that his own sister and two other women be received back to communion (Ep. XX)

voices.hedge: These letters survive only because Cyprian kept them, though they cut against his own case. Celerinus never names his sister. No word of hers survives.
voices.text: Celerinus was a confessor of Carthage. He had been put in prison and had not denied Christ. His letter to Lucian, another confessor in prison, survives with Lucian's reply. In it he grieves for his sister, who had sacrificed, and asks Lucian to help restore her. Neither man was yet a cleric. These two letters are the clearest lay voices this world kept.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

voices.hedge: So much of Augustine survives that he can seem to be this world's whole voice. He is not. He was one bishop, writing about the people in front of him, and their own words mostly did not survive.
voices.text: Augustine came to the faith in 386 and was baptized at Milan in 387. In 391 the congregation at Hippo seized him and had him made a presbyter while he wept. He was bishop there from 395 or 396 until his death in 430. He preached, taught those preparing for baptism, and argued against the Donatists, the Manichaeans and the Pelagians. Until his last illness he did not stop preaching.

dates.display: Augustine's own friend for nearly forty years; bishop of Calama in his own right; physically present at Augustine's deathbed in 430, one of those Augustine 'asked of us who were present'; wrote the Vita Augustini, the source for the psalms on the wall and for the account of the people seizing Augustine at Hippo

voices.hedge: Possidius is the only witness to Augustine's last weeks. He wrote as an admirer. Even so, his account of the death carries no wonders and no signs from above.
voices.text: Possidius was bishop of Calama and Augustine's friend for nearly forty years. He wrote the Life of Augustine. He was in the house at Hippo during the siege of 430, and he watched and prayed as Augustine died.

tile.text: From about 246 to 430, this was the ordinary church of two cities in Roman North Africa, Carthage and Hippo. Each congregation had one bishop, given a particular people and answerable for them. When a persecution in 250 made many of them give way, their bishop did not write them off. He set a road back, examined and walked in the open. Cyprian of Carthage held that road, and he was put to death in 258. A century and a half later, Augustine of Hippo argued that Cyprian had been wrong about baptism, but never called him an outsider. This church argued hard about the font, about councils and about grace, but always inside a bond it would not break. Both bishops speak at length in their own words. Almost everyone else is missing: the ordinary believer, the women, and the people who gave way.
